claims.text: The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi films or nanoribbons possess significant interfacial strain and microstructural disorder.
Processing-induced interfacial strain largely governs the magnetocaloric response of these low-dimensional FeMnNiGeSi alloys.
Interfacial strain enhances local magnetic anisotropy.
Interfacial strain and associated defects cause magnetic domain-wall pinning.
Strain-induced anisotropy and domain-wall pinning limit reversible magnetic-moment reorientation during low-field cycling.
The low-dimensional state can exhibit a lower maximum magnetic entropy change than a bulk counterpart.
The nanoscale state can broaden the effective temperature range of the entropy-change response.
Strain and disorder increase magnetic hysteresis in the as-deposited material.
A moderate post-deposition anneal will partially relax interfacial strain.
A moderate post-deposition anneal will homogenize the film or nanoribbon microstructure.
Annealing-induced strain relaxation will reduce domain-wall pinning and permit more coherent magnetic reorientation.
Relative to the as-deposited baseline, annealed samples will show a sharper magnetic-entropy-change peak.
Relative to the as-deposited baseline, annealed samples will show reduced M-H hysteresis under low applied fields.
Strain relaxation may improve effective cooling-cycle frequency by improving heat-transfer response.
The proposed comparison is to be conducted at fields up to 1–2 T near the magnetocaloric transition.
The proposed operating regime covers nanoscale films or nanoribbons approximately 10–100 nm thick, with the broader boundary extending to a few hundred nanometers.
Substrate interactions and film thickness may alter how much strain annealing can relax.
Microstructural disorder may contribute beneficially to the breadth of the entropy-change response, creating a competing effect during annealing.
